\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUMMARIES OF A STOCHASTIC PROCESS}}

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{6} \textbf{Summaries:} 

Note that these are \textbf{population characteristics} of the stochastic process. Their sample counterparts are non-parametric estimators, since we do not impose a specific parametric structure on the process (e.g.\ $Y_t=\alpha+\beta x_t+\varepsilon_t$).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Mean function (Sample mean)}  $\mu : t \mapsto \mu(t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t],  t = 1, 2, \dots$. For a weakly stationary time series, the population mean is constant, $\mu(t)\equiv\mu$, and it can be estimated by the sample mean, that is unbiased, and under ergodicity, consistent. \textcolor{orange}{\textbf{Exam (June 2022 Q1):} is the sample mean }$\bar Y_n$\textcolor{orange}{ an appropriate estimator of }$\mathbb{E}[Y_n]$\textcolor{orange}{? \textbf{Yes, only under conditions.} In general \emph{no}: a single realization gives only \emph{one} datum at each time, and }$\mathbb{E}[Y_n]=\mu(n)$\textcolor{orange}{ may vary with }$t$\textcolor{orange}{, so averaging mixes variables with different means. It is appropriate under \emph{weak stationarity} (then }$\mu(n)\equiv\mu$\textcolor{orange}{ and }$\bar Y_n$\textcolor{orange}{ is unbiased) \emph{plus ergodicity} (then the time average is consistent, }$\bar Y_n\to\mu$\textcolor{orange}{).}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Variance function}  $\sigma^2 : t \mapsto \sigma^2(t) = \mathrm{Var}(Y_t),  t = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocovariance function}  $\gamma : (t, t') \mapsto \gamma(t, t') = \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t'}), $\quad$  t, t' = 1, 2, \dots$

$$
\gamma(t,t')=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t'})=\mathbb{E}\big[(Y_t-\mu(t))(Y_{t'}-\mu(t'))\big]
$$

However, for a \emph{stationary} process, the covariance depends only on the lag $h = t' - t$:
$$ \gamma(h) \;=\; \operatorname{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}). $$

\textcolor{orange}{\textbf{Exam (May 2025 Q1a): ``the acf can be defined only if the series is stationary?'' --- No.} The autocovariance } $\gamma(t,t')=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t'})$ \textcolor{orange}{ is well defined for \emph{any} process with finite second moments; stationarity is \emph{not} needed to \emph{define} it. Stationarity only makes it depend on the lag } $h=t'-t$ \textcolor{orange}{ alone (giving }$\gamma(h)$\textcolor{orange}{), and only then is the correlogram a consistent estimator of it (that is Q1b).}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation function}  $\rho : (t, t') \mapsto \rho(t, t') = \mathrm{Corr}(Y_t, Y_{t'}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t'})}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(Y_t)\,\mathrm{Var}(Y_{t'})}}, $\quad$  t, t' = 1, 2, \dots$
For a stationary process: 
$$
\rho(t,t+h)
=
\frac{\gamma(h)}{\sqrt{\sigma^2\sigma^2}}
=
\frac{\gamma(h)}{\gamma(0)}.
$$
\textbf{Correlogram.} This is just the ACF esimated on the sample!  
$$ \hat\rho(h) \;=\; \frac{\hat\gamma(h)}{\hat\gamma(0)}. $$
The correlogram can estimate the acf only if the series is stationary: the sample acf averages over time== FOR A GIVEN LAG== (this is the issue!), so it consistently estimates the acf only under weak stationarity plus ergodicity
\end{keydef}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 2 --- CATEGORICAL TIME SERIES (PANEL ON VOTE INTENTION)}}

**14** Only the things in yellow! 
Usual assumptions.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Common setup (preamble, shared by all sub-exercises below).}}

\emph{States:} $1$ = Rep., $2$ = Dem., $3$ = Don't know.

\emph{Transition matrix} $\mathbf P$ (given as data for the exercises):

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t-1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ (Rep.) & $2$ (Dem.) & $3$ (Don't know) \\
\hline
$1$ (Rep.)        & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\
$2$ (Dem.)        & $0.1$ & $0.7$ & $0.2$ \\
$3$ (Don't know)  & $0.0$ & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\emph{Initial state:} at $t = 0$, the person is undecided, $Y_0 = 3$. Note we have no $p_0$ here! (better, it is deterministic!) So $\boldsymbol\pi_0 = (0, 0, 1)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Master tools (used by every row of the table below).}} For any homogeneous Markov chain:

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{14} $$ \boxed{\;\text{(M1) Marginal recursion: }\; \boldsymbol\pi_{n+1} = \boldsymbol\pi_n\, \mathbf P. \;} $$
\end{keydef}

\emph{Compute the $\boldsymbol\pi_n$'s once, reuse everywhere below:}
$$ \boldsymbol\pi_1 \;=\; \boldsymbol\pi_0\, \mathbf P \;=\; (0,\, 0.4,\, 0.6) \quad\text{(row $3$ of $\mathbf P$)}, $$
$$ \boldsymbol\pi_2 \;=\; \boldsymbol\pi_1\,  \mathbf P \;=\; (\,0.04,\, 0.52,\, 0.44\,), \qquad \boldsymbol\pi_3 \;=\; \boldsymbol\pi_2\, \mathbf P \;=\; (\,0.076,\, 0.552,\, 0.372\,). $$

Notice this multiplicaiton is like row by column, and you do the first element of the row * the first element of the column, the second element of the row * the second element of the column etc... and then you start again, from the second column this time!

Note: the generic forula pi t+1 = pi t * P can give me the codnitonal version if i just consider the conditional initial p and transition p? is like a reduciton int he dimensiosn i  am using

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked sub-exercises --- unified in one table (1 row per exercise, all formulas preserved).}}

\begin{tabular}{p{6cm}|p{8cm}|p{16cm}|p{8cm}}
\hline
\textbf{Sub-exercise} & \textbf{Tool  and  rationale} & \textbf{Full computation} & \textbf{Result} \\
\hline
\textbf{(b) Joint} \;\;\; $P(Y_1 = 3,\, Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3)$
& Joints are not marginals --- use the chain rule (M2) directly, not the $\boldsymbol\pi$-recursion.
& $P(Y_1 = 3,\, Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) \;=\; p_{3,3}\, p_{3,2} \;=\; 0.6 \times 0.4$ you see is a dimensionality reduction! 
& $\boxed{0.24}$
\\
\hline
\textbf{(c) Marginal} \;\;\; $P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3)$
& Just the $2$nd entry of $\boldsymbol\pi_2$ (M1).
& $P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) \;=\; \pi_2(2)$
& $\boxed{0.52}$
\\
\hline
\textbf{(d) Conditional} \;\;\; $P(Y_1 = 3 \mid Y_2 = 2,\, Y_0 = 3)$
& Bayes (M3) $=$ joint $/$ marginal $=$ (b) $/$ (c).
& $P(Y_1 = 3 \mid Y_2 = 2,\, Y_0 = 3) \;=\; \dfrac{P(Y_1 = 3,\, Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3)}{P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3)} \;=\; \dfrac{0.24}{0.52}$
& $\boxed{\approx 0.462}$
\\
\hline
\textbf{(e1) Full distribution of $Y_2 \mid Y_0 = 3$}
& Read off $\boldsymbol\pi_2$ above (M1).
& $\boldsymbol\pi_2 \;=\; (\,\underbrace{0.04}_{P(Y_2 = 1)},\, \underbrace{0.52}_{P(Y_2 = 2)},\, \underbrace{0.44}_{P(Y_2 = 3)}\,)$
& $\boxed{(0.04,\, 0.52,\, 0.44)}$
\\
\hline
\textbf{(e2) Full distribution of $Y_3 \mid Y_0 = 3$}
& Read off $\boldsymbol\pi_3$ above (M1).
& $\boldsymbol\pi_3 \;=\; (\,\underbrace{0.076}_{P(Y_3 = 1)},\, \underbrace{0.552}_{P(Y_3 = 2)},\, \underbrace{0.372}_{P(Y_3 = 3)}\,)$
& $\boxed{(0.076,\, 0.552,\, 0.372)}$
\\
\hline
\end{tabular}

Note that d is just the definition of conditional probability + extra conditioning: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \and B)}{P(B)}   $$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATE SPACE MODELS (SSM)}}



\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{21a} \textbf{State-space model (SSM).} An SSM is a dynamic system of stochastic processes:
$$ \bigl(\, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{observation}},\; \underbrace{\theta_t}_{\text{latent}} \textcolor{blue}{(S_t)} \,\bigr)_{t \ge 1}, \quad \text{starting at } \theta_0 \textcolor{blue}{(S_0)}, $$
where the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} state process $(\theta_t)$ In particular :

$\bullet$ $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$ **is a Markov process** with continuous state space $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$ \textcolor{blue}{(\emph{finite discrete} state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$)}, initial distribution $\pi$ and transition kernel $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ (\textcolor{blue}{transition \emph{matrix} $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$, $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$}).
$\bullet$ Given $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are **conditionally independent** and each $Y_t$ **depends only on** $\theta_t$: $$ p(y_t \mid \theta_{0:t}, y_{1:t-1}) = p(y_t \mid \theta_t). $$
In summary: $\omark{Y_t = h_t(\theta_t, v_t), \; \theta_t = g_t(\theta_{t-1}, w_t)}$

The law of an SSM is fully specified by (\textcolor{blue}{finite discrete / HMM version in blue parentheses}):
$$ \theta_0 \;\sim\; \underbrace{\pi}_{\text{initial law}}\ \textcolor{blue}{\bigl(S_0 \sim \pi\bigr)}, \qquad \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \;\sim\; \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})}_{\text{transition kernel}}\ \textcolor{blue}{\bigl(S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \sim \mathrm{Categorical}(p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M})\bigr)}, \qquad Y_t \mid \theta_t \;\sim\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)}_{\text{emission kernel}}\ \textcolor{blue}{\bigl(Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(y_t \mid \theta_j^*)\bigr)}. $$
\end{keydef}




\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Example of Parametric emission --- Poisson emissions.}} In other cases one may want a parametric emission distribution, so that $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$, $j = 1, \dots, K$. For example, for the earthquakes data (unbounded counts), one could assume
$$ Y_t \mid (S_t = j) \;\sim\; \text{Poisson}(\theta_j^*), $$
that is, at state $j$, $Y_t$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\theta_j^*$. Note how the parameter can switch across states!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this fixes the plain-Poisson defects.}} A single Poisson forces (i) mean $=$ variance (no overdispersion), (ii) no serial dependence. Letting the rate \emph{switch} with a Markov chain breaks both:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Different mean and variance per regime.} Within state $j$, both equal $\lambda_j^*$, but across regimes they differ --- a "quiet" state has small mean \emph{and} small variance, an "active" one has large mean \emph{and} large variance.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation.} Sticky regimes ($p_{j,j}$ near $1$) mean neighbouring $Y_t$'s likely share the same rate, so
$$ \text{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \text{Cov}(\lambda_{S_t}^*, \lambda_{S_{t+h}}^*) \;>\; 0. $$
No additive $\epsilon$ needed --- the dependence comes from persistence of the hidden chain.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WRITE YOUR OWN MODEL --- build any DLM in 5 moves.}}



\textbf{1. How many series do you observe? $\rightarrow q$.} One dependent variable $\Rightarrow q=1$ (univariate); $m$ stacked series $\Rightarrow q=m$, $Y_t\in\mathbb{R}^m$.

\textbf{2. How many states, and are they coupled? $\rightarrow p$ and $G$.} Pick the state dimension $p$, then ask: do you want state 1 to be affected by state 2 (\emph{joint}) or not (\emph{separate})? Coupling is exactly the off-diagonal of $G$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{$p=2$, joint:} $\theta_{1,t}=\theta_{1,t-1}+\theta_{2,t-1}+w_{\theta_1,t}$, $\theta_{2,t}=\theta_{2,t-1}+w_{\theta_2,t}$ $\Rightarrow$ $G=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\cr0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (the $1$ in slot $(1,2)$ feeds $\theta_2$ into $\theta_1$).
\item \textbf{$p=2$, separate:} $\theta_{1,t}=\theta_{1,t-1}+w_{\theta_1,t}$, $\theta_{2,t}=\theta_{2,t-1}+w_{\theta_2,t}$ $\Rightarrow$ $G=I_2=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\cr0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
\item \textbf{$p=4$, joint (two coupled blocks):} $\theta=(\theta^a_1,\theta^a_2,\theta^b_1,\theta^b_2)$, each block a joint pair $\Rightarrow$ $G=\mathrm{blkdiag}\!\left(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\cr0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr),\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\cr0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\right)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&0&0\cr0&1&0&0\cr0&0&1&1\cr0&0&0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
\item \textbf{$p=4$, separate:} each state its own random walk $\Rightarrow$ $G=I_4$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{3. State noise $\rightarrow W$.} $w_t\sim\mathcal{N}_p(0,W)$.
\begin{itemize}
\item 2 states: $W_{2\times2}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma^2_{w_{\theta_1}}&\sigma_{w_{\theta_1}w_{\theta_2}}\cr\sigma_{w_{\theta_1}w_{\theta_2}}&\sigma^2_{w_{\theta_2}}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ --- off-diagonal $=$ correlated shocks (set $0$ for independent; set a whole row/column to $0$ to \emph{freeze} that state, giving a singular $W$).
\item 4 states: block-diagonal $W_{4\times4}=\mathrm{blkdiag}(W_{\theta_1},W_{\theta_2})=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\ast&\ast&0&0\cr\ast&\ast&0&0\cr0&0&\ast&\ast\cr0&0&\ast&\ast\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ --- each $2\times2$ block couples the \emph{same} component across the two series ("borrowing strength").
\end{itemize}

\textbf{4. Observation noise $\rightarrow V$.} $v_t\sim\mathcal{N}_q(0,V)$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $q=1$: $V_{1\times1}=\sigma^2_v$ (scalar).
\item $q=2$: $V_{2\times2}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma^2_{v_1}&\sigma_{v_{12}}\cr\sigma_{v_{12}}&\sigma^2_{v_2}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ --- off-diagonal $=$ contemporaneous cross-series measurement correlation. (Set $V=0$ when the state \emph{is} the observation, e.g. AR / VAR.)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{5. What combination do you observe? $\rightarrow F$.} $F$ (size $q\times p$) extracts the observed mix; use a placeholder $k\in\{1,\ t,\ x_t,\ \text{dummy}\}$ --- constant, time trend, covariate, or seasonal dummy.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{$p=2$, extract only the first state:} $F=(k,\ 0)$.
\item \textbf{$p=2$, extract both states:} $F=(k,\ k)$ (e.g. level $+$ slope$\cdot k$; use $(1,\ x_t)$ for a regression).
\item \textbf{$p=4$, extract the first of each block ($q=2$):} $F=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}k&0&0&0\cr0&0&k&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
\item \textbf{$p=4$, extract both per block ($q=2$):} $F=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&k&0&0\cr0&0&1&k\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
\end{itemize}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MASTER TABLE --- every DLM from simplest to composite (buildup).}}




\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{21c}
\begin{tabular}{p{4.4cm}|p{6.6cm}|p{8.8cm}|p{5.6cm}|p{6.6cm}|p{3.2cm}|p{4.8cm}|p{2cm}}
\textbf{Model --- what it adds} & \textbf{$q$; observation eq.\ $Y_t$} & \textbf{$p$, joint/separate; state eq.\ $\theta_t$} & \textbf{$G$ (from $\theta_t=G\theta_{t-1}+w_t$)} where these objects can have multiple rows, and where in the present you need the full rhs, in the past you just have the vectors & \textbf{$W$ (state noise)} & \textbf{$V$ (obs noise)} & \textbf{$F$} & \textbf{Asked} \\
\hline
\textbf{RW + noise} (local level). \emph{The atom: a single random-walk level seen through noise.} & $q=1$. $Y_t=\mu_t+v_t$. & $p=1$.\newline $\mu_t=\mu_{t-1}+w_{\mu,t}$ & $G=1$. & $W=\sigma^2_{w\mu}$. & $V=\sigma^2_v$. & $F=1$. & \textcolor[HTML]{e08635}{\textbf{6}} \\
\hline
\textbf{LLT} (local linear trend). \emph{Adds a slope state so the level drifts.} & $q=1$. $Y_t=\mu_t+v_t$. & $p=2$ JOINT.\newline $\mu_t=\mu_{t-1}+\textcolor{blue}{\beta_{t-1}}+w_{\mu,t}$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+w_{\beta,t}}$ & $G=\begin{pmatrix}1&\textcolor{blue}{1}\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. & $W=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2_{w\mu},\textcolor{blue}{\sigma^2_{w\beta}})$. & $V=\sigma^2_v$. & $F=(1,\ 0)$. & \textcolor[HTML]{5aa469}{\textbf{1}} \\
\hline
\textcolor{gray}{\textbf{RW + drift}. \emph{Freezes the LLT slope: constant drift.}} & $q=1$. $Y_t=\mu_t+v_t$. & $p=2$ JOINT.\newline $\mu_t=\mu_{t-1}+\beta_{t-1}+w_{\mu,t}$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\beta_t=\beta_{t-1}}$ & $G=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. & $W=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^2_{w\mu}&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ \textcolor{blue}{singular}. & $V=\sigma^2_v$. & $F=(1,\ 0)$. & \textcolor[HTML]{9aa0a6}{\textbf{0}} \\
\hline
\textbf{DLR / dynamic CAPM}. & $q=1$. $Y_t=\alpha_t+\textcolor{blue}{\beta_t x_t}+v_t$. & $p=2$ \textcolor{blue}{SEPARATE}.\newline $\alpha_t=\alpha_{t-1}+w_{\alpha,t}$\newline $\beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+w_{\beta,t}$ & $G=I_2$. & $W=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2_{w\alpha},\sigma^2_{w\beta})$. & $V=\sigma^2_v$. & $F=(1,\ \textcolor{blue}{x_t})$. & \textcolor[HTML]{d6453f}{\textbf{8}} \\
\hline
\textcolor{gray}{\textbf{Fixed reg (OLS)}. \emph{Static regression as a degenerate DLM.}} & $q=1$. $Y_t=\alpha+\beta x_t+v_t$. & $p=2$ SEPARATE.\newline $\alpha_t=\alpha$\newline $\beta_t=\beta$ \textcolor{blue}{(frozen)} & $G=I_2$. & $\textcolor{blue}{W=0}$. & $V=\sigma^2_v$. & $F=(1,\ x_t)$. & \textcolor[HTML]{5aa469}{\textbf{1}} \\
\hline
\textbf{SUR}. \emph{Two DLRs in parallel, linked through correlated errors (Zellner).} & $q=2$. $Y_{1,t}=\alpha_{1,t}+\beta_{1,t}x_t+v_{1,t}$; $\textcolor{blue}{Y_{2,t}=\alpha_{2,t}+\beta_{2,t}x_t+v_{2,t}}$. & $p=4$ SEPARATE, \textcolor{blue}{state grouped by type $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\beta_1,\beta_2)$}.\newline $\alpha_{1,t}=\alpha_{1,t-1}+w_{\alpha 1,t}$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\alpha_{2,t}=\alpha_{2,t-1}+w_{\alpha 2,t}}$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\beta_{1,t}=\beta_{1,t-1}+w_{\beta 1,t}}$\newline $\beta_{2,t}=\beta_{2,t-1}+w_{\beta 2,t}$ & $G=I_4$. & $W=\mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$ \textcolor{blue}{(now genuinely block-diagonal in this order)} with $W_\alpha=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^2_{\alpha1}&\textcolor{blue}{\sigma_\alpha}\\\textcolor{blue}{\sigma_\alpha}&\sigma^2_{\alpha2}\end{pmatrix}$, $W_\beta$ analogous. & $V=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^2_{v1}&\textcolor{blue}{\sigma_v}\\\textcolor{blue}{\sigma_v}&\sigma^2_{v2}\end{pmatrix}$. & $F=\textcolor{blue}{\begin{pmatrix}1&0&x_t&0\\0&1&0&x_t\end{pmatrix}}$. & \textcolor[HTML]{9aa0a6}{\textbf{0}} \\
\hline
\textbf{SUTSE}. \emph{Two LLTs sharing information through correlated level shocks --- borrowing strength. (May 2025 Q4d; June 2026 Q6b.)} & $q=2$. $Y_{1,t}=\mu_{1,t}+v_{1,t}$; $Y_{2,t}=\mu_{2,t}+v_{2,t}$. & $p=4$ \textcolor{blue}{JOINT}, \textcolor{blue}{state grouped by type $(\mu_1,\mu_2,\beta_1,\beta_2)$}. two LLTs:\newline $\mu_{1,t}=\mu_{1,t-1}+\beta_{1,t-1}+w_{\mu 1,t}$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\mu_{2,t}=\mu_{2,t-1}+\beta_{2,t-1}+w_{\mu 2,t}}$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\beta_{1,t}=\beta_{1,t-1}+w_{\beta 1,t}}$\newline $\beta_{2,t}=\beta_{2,t-1}+w_{\beta 2,t}$ & $G=\textcolor{blue}{\begin{pmatrix}I_2&I_2\\0&I_2\end{pmatrix}}$ \textcolor{blue}{(each $\mu_i$ carries its own $\beta_i$)}. & $W=\mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\mu,W_\beta)$, $W_\mu=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^2_{\mu1}&\textcolor{blue}{\sigma_\mu}\\\textcolor{blue}{\sigma_\mu}&\sigma^2_{\mu2}\end{pmatrix}$, $W_\beta$ analogous. & $V=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^2_{v1}&\sigma_v\\\sigma_v&\sigma^2_{v2}\end{pmatrix}$. & $F=\textcolor{blue}{\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&0\end{pmatrix}}$. & \textcolor[HTML]{e08635}{\textbf{6}} \\
\hline
\textbf{AR(1)}. \emph{State == observation; autoregressive ($|\varphi|<1$ stationary).} & $q=1$. $Y_t=\theta_t$ ($V=0\Rightarrow\theta_t\equiv Y_t$). & $p=1$ SEPARATE.\newline $\theta_t=\varphi\theta_{t-1}+w_t$\newline \textcolor{blue}{Since $\theta_t=Y_t$ ($V=0$), so $\theta_{t-1}=Y_{t-1}$, this is exactly $Y_t=\varphi Y_{t-1}+w_t$.} & $\textcolor{blue}{G=\varphi}$. & $W=\sigma^2_w$. & $\textcolor{blue}{V=0}$. & $F=1$. & \textcolor[HTML]{b39412}{\textbf{3}} \\
\hline
\textbf{AR(2)} (companion). \emph{Two lags $\Rightarrow$ not Markov in $Y$ alone; add auxiliary state. June 2024 Q2 trap: $F$ must be constant, so putting $Y_{t-1},Y_{t-2}$ in $F$ is NOT a valid DLM.} & $q=1$. $Y_t=\theta_{1,t}$ ($V=0$). & $p=2$ JOINT.\newline $\theta_{1,t}=\phi_1\theta_{1,t-1}+\theta_{2,t-1}+w_t$\newline $\textcolor{blue}{\theta_{2,t}=\phi_2\theta_{1,t-1}}$\newline \textcolor{blue}{Here $\theta_{1,t}=Y_t$ (so $\theta_{1,t-1}=Y_{t-1}$), and $\theta_{2,t}=\phi_2\theta_{1,t-1}=\phi_2 Y_{t-1}\Rightarrow\theta_{2,t-1}=\phi_2 Y_{t-2}$. Substituting into the first line: $Y_t=\phi_1 Y_{t-1}+\phi_2 Y_{t-2}+w_t$ (the AR(2) recursion).} & $G=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_1&\textcolor{blue}{1}\\\textcolor{blue}{\phi_2}&\textcolor{blue}{0}\end{pmatrix}$ companion. & $W=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ singular. & $V=0$. & $F=(1,\ 0)$. & \textcolor[HTML]{5aa469}{\textbf{1}} \\
\hline
\textbf{VAR(1)} (bivariate). \emph{AR(1) for $q=2$ with full cross-lag coupling. (Not in DLMwR; state-space absorbs it via a full $G$.)} & $q=2$. $(Y_{1,t},Y_{2,t})^\top=\theta_t$ ($V=0$). & $p=2$ JOINT.\newline $\theta_{1,t}=\phi_{11}\theta_{1,t-1}+\textcolor{blue}{\phi_{12}\theta_{2,t-1}}+w_t^{(1)}$\newline $\theta_{2,t}=\textcolor{blue}{\phi_{21}\theta_{1,t-1}}+\phi_{22}\theta_{2,t-1}+w_t^{(2)}$ & $G=\Phi=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{11}&\textcolor{blue}{\phi_{12}}\\\textcolor{blue}{\phi_{21}}&\phi_{22}\end{pmatrix}$. & $W=\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_1^2&\sigma_{12}\\\sigma_{12}&\sigma_2^2\end{pmatrix}$. & $V=0$. & $F=I_2$. & \textcolor[HTML]{9aa0a6}{\textbf{0}} \\
\hline
\textcolor{orange}{\textbf{Dynamic common factors} (dimension reduction). \emph{$m$ series driven by $p<m$ shared latent factors --- state SMALLER than obs. Instance $m=3$, $p=1$. nodes.title: SSM flexibility — no stationarity required
Example 2: AR(1)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 3 --- AR(1), continuous-state Markov (A: directly observed; B: SSM lift).}}

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{11} Steps:
\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} Discrete-time Markov process on $\mathbb{R}$:
$$ Y_t \;=\; \varphi\, Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). $$
Note the use of big Y as this is a structural statement.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof: $|\varphi| < 1$ $\Rightarrow$ weakly stationary.}} Unroll the recursion from $Y_0$:
$$ Y_t \;=\; \varphi^t Y_0 \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, \varepsilon_{t-k}. $$
\emph{1.\ Constant mean.}
$$ E[Y_t] \;=\; \underbrace{\varphi^t\, E[Y_0]}_{\to 0 } \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\ }_{\frac{1-\varphi^t}{1-\varphi}} E[\varepsilon_{t-k}]  \;=\; 0 $$
\emph{2.\ Constant, finite variance.} By independence of shocks and $Y_0$:
$$ \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \underbrace{\varphi^{2t}\, \mathrm{Var}(Y_0)}_{\to 0 } \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^{2k} \sigma^2 \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{1-\varphi^2} \qquad \text{for all } t. \quad \checkmark $$
Note how you could have started also from a non-stationary Y0 and gained asymptotic stationarity
\emph{3.\ Autocovariance depends only on lag $h$.} For $h \ge 0$:
$$ \gamma(h) \;:=\; \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \varphi^h\, \gamma(0). $$No $t$-dependence. \quad $\checkmark$
depends only on the lag! 
\emph{Autocorrelation:} $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0) = \varphi^{h}$
\end{keydef}

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 1 --- Simple random walk.}}

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{10} \textbf{Steps} - A player starts with capital $y_0 = 0$, **deterministic**. 
- Assume $\varepsilon_t \underbrace{\sim}_{iid} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ (Gaussian RW; \emph{the increments $\varepsilon_t$ are iid, NOT the $Y_t$ themselves --- $Y_t$ is a cumulative sum so $Y_t$ depends on $Y_{t-1}$}):\[ Y_t \;=\; Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \;=\; y_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{t} \varepsilon_k. \]
$\varepsilon_t$ iid and independent of past $Y$'s $\Rightarrow$ $Y_t$ is Markov

\[ E[Y_t] \;=\; E\Bigl[\sum_{k=1}^{t} \varepsilon_k\Bigr] \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{t} E[\varepsilon_k] \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{t} 0 \;=\; 0. \]

\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\sum_{s=1}^{t} \varepsilon_s\Bigr) \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{t} \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_s) \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{t} \sigma^2 \;=\; t\sigma^2. \]
\emph{Variance grows linearly in $t$} (standard deviation widens as $\sqrt{t}$),



 so the walk is \textbf{non-stationary} (note $V(Y_0) = 0$  because $y_0$ is fixed deterministic). The variance of the random walk explodes in time. 


\emph{Continuous-time limit} (small steps in rapid succession): \textbf{Brownian motion}. The recursion works for any iid $\varepsilon_t$, not just $\pm 1$.
\end{keydef}

nodes.title: Bayesian point estimation: loss functions and the posterior mean
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN POINT ESTIMATION.}}
After obtaining the posterior $f(\theta\mid y)$, a Bayes point estimator is chosen to minimize the posterior expected loss:
$$
\boxed{\hat a^*=\arg\min_a E[L(\theta,a)\mid y]
=\arg\min_a\int L(\theta,a)f(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta.}
$$
The optimal estimator depends on the loss function: squared loss gives the \textbf{posterior mean} (to minimize squared loss you take the mean), absolute loss the \textbf{posterior median}.

Is this a dlm or an ssm?
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Exam --- Is it a SSM? Is it a DLM? (nonlinear observation eq.).}} A recurring exam task gives a model and asks whether it is a state-space process and whether it is a DLM. Take the stochastic-volatility model for financial returns $Y_t = \exp(\theta_t/2)\, v_t, \; v_t \sim N(0,1), \qquad \theta_t = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \; w_t \sim N(0,\sigma^2),$ with $\theta_t$ a non-observable AR(1).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Yes, it IS a state-space process.} The latent $(\theta_t)$ is a Markov process (an AR(1): $\theta_t$ depends on the past only through $\theta_{t-1}$), and conditionally on $\theta_t$ the observation $Y_t$ depends only on $\theta_t$ (through its own independent noise $v_t$). It is exactly the book's general SSM form $Y_t = h_t(\theta_t, v_t), \; \theta_t = g_t(\theta_{t-1}, w_t)$ with $h_t(\theta_t, v_t) = \exp(\theta_t/2)\, v_t$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{No, it is NOT a DLM.} A DLM needs the linear-Gaussian observation equation $Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t, \; Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim N(F_t \theta_t, V_t)$.
Here the observation equation is nonlinear in the state: the state enters through $\exp(\theta_t/2)$ and multiplies the noise, giving $Y_t \mid \theta_t \sim N(0,\, e^{\theta_t})$ --- the conditional mean is $0$ (not $F_t \theta_t$) and the state acts nonlinearly on the variance. The state equation $\theta_t = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 \theta_{t-1} + w_t$
IS linear-Gaussian, but a DLM requires BOTH equations linear-Gaussian; the observation equation fails, so the model is a (nonlinear) state-space model but not a DLM.

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Markov chains are (not) stationary.}}

\textcolor{orange}{
\textbf{``Markov chains are stationary'' --- NO.}
}

A homogeneous Markov chain need not be stationary.

For example, consider the deterministic flip chain on $\{1,2\}$:
$$
p_{12}=p_{21}=1,
\qquad
Y_0=1.
$$

Then
$$
P(Y_t=1)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&t\text{ even},\\
0,&t\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus the marginal distribution changes with $t$, so the process is not
stationary.



For the flip chain,
$$
\pi=(1/2,1/2).
$$

nodes.title: Exercise — weather/activity filtering (state is unobserved)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXERCISE --- Filtering: weather $\to$ activity}}


\textbf{Setup.} A person's daily activity depends on the weather, which is hidden. We observe only the activity.

$\bullet$ Hidden $\mathcal{S} = \{1 = \text{sunny},\, 2 = \text{rainy}\}$ ($K = 2$), observed $\mathcal{Y} = \{1 = \text{walk},\, 2 = \text{shop},\, 3 = \text{clean}\}$ ($M = 3$).

$\bullet$ Initial $\pi = (P(S_1 = \text{sunny}), P(S_1 = \text{rainy})) = (0.6,\, 0.4)$.

\textbf{Transition matrix} $A$ (rows = state at $t-1$, columns = state at $t$):
\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{7cm}|p{7cm}} $t-1 \backslash t$ & sunny & rainy \\ \hline sunny & $0.7$ & $0.3$ \\ rainy & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{Emission matrix} $B$ (rows = state, columns = activity):
\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{7cm}|p{7cm}|p{7cm}} $S_t \backslash Y_t$ & walk & shop & clean \\ \hline sunny & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\ rainy & $0.1$ & $0.4$ & $0.5$ \end{tabular}


Just think at priors and posteriors: 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(a) After $y_1 = \text{walk}$.}} No transition needed yet (start of chain):
$$ \alpha_1(\text{sunny}) = \pi_{\text{sunny}}\, b_{\text{sunny, walk}} = 0.6 \cdot 0.6 = 0.36, \qquad \alpha_1(\text{rainy}) = 0.4 \cdot 0.1 = 0.04. $$
Walking is far more compatible with sunny ($0.6$ vs $0.1$) $\Rightarrow$ score ratio $9{:}1$ in favour of sunny.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(b) After $y_2 = \text{shop}$.}}

\emph{Predict $S_2$ from history:} push $\alpha_1$ through $A$:
$$ \text{pred}_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.7 + 0.04 \cdot 0.4 = 0.268, \qquad \text{pred}_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.3 + 0.04 \cdot 0.6 = 0.132. $$
\emph{Weight by today's emission:}
$$ \alpha_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.268 \cdot 0.3 = 0.0804, \qquad \alpha_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.132 \cdot 0.4 = 0.0528. $$
Shopping is mildly more compatible with rainy ($0.4$ vs $0.3$), pulling the belief from $9{:}1$ down to roughly $1.5{:}1$; sunny stays ahead because the chain is sticky ($p_{\text{sunny}, \text{sunny}} = 0.7$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ Two-step recipe at every $t$: (1) push the old belief through $A$ to get the predicted prior; (2) multiply by the emission to fold in today's evidence.

$\bullet$ $\alpha_t(j) = P(S_t = j, y_{1:t})$ is a \emph{joint}, not a posterior. Their relative magnitudes already tell you which state is more likely; summing them gives the data likelihood $P(y_{1:t}) = \sum_j \alpha_t(j)$ for free.

$\bullet$ This is exactly the \emph{forward algorithm} --- the engine inside HMM likelihood evaluation, filtering, and (with a small modification: $\max$ instead of $\sum$) Viterbi decoding.

nodes.title: Decoding / filtering
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{27} 
Estimate the latent state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given observed $y_{1:T}$ (treat $s_0$ as fixed, and $\phi$ as known or replaced by its MLE).


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, pick the marginally most likely state:
$$ s_t^* \;=\; \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s), \qquad \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). $$
\emph{Issue.} The resulting sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may include zero-probability transitions ($p_{i,j} = 0$), making the global path infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the path that maximises the joint conditional probability:
$$ \max_{s_{0:T}} p(s_0, \dots, s_T \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). $$
Given the data, and the parameters, what is the most likely hidden state \textcolor{orange}{\emph{path}}?
\end{keydef}

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
$$ \begin{aligned} & p(s_0, \dots, s_T,\, y_1, \dots, y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} p(s_0, \dots, s_T \mid y_1, \dots, y_T, \phi)\, p(y_1, \dots, y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} $$
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $p(s_0, \dots, s_T,\, y_1, \dots, y_T \mid \phi)$ with respect to $s_{0:T}$ (with $\phi$ fixed). \;Same maximiser, easier expression.

\medskip

nodes.title: Application
nodes.content:
\textbf{Application: point estimate of an election probability.}



}







Data: a panel is interviewed monthly from January ($t=0$) to June ($t=5$), with states



$$



1=\text{YES},



\qquad



2=\text{NO},



\qquad



3=\text{Uncertain}.



$$







Target:



$$



\boxed{



q



=



P(\text{July YES share}>50\%).



}



$$







The exam table is a \emph{pooled transition-count table}: its entries are the $n_{ij}$ above, summed over all observed transitions.







Its grand total is



$$



500=100\times5



$$



under the interpretation of $100$ chains observed across five transitions.







The row totals



$$



(n_{1,+},n_{2,+},n_{3,+})



=



(150,250,100)



$$



therefore count pooled \emph{departures} from the three states.







They are not the June state counts.







\textbf{Step 1 --- counts-ratio MLEs.}







From



$$



\hat p_{ij}



=



\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i,+}},



$$



the estimated transition probabilities into YES are



$$



\frac{70}{150}=0.467,



\qquad



\frac{75}{250}=0.300,



\qquad



\frac{30}{100}=0.300.



$$







If the pooled occupancy proportions are used as a proxy for the current state distribution, one-step propagation gives



$$



\boxed{



\hat p_{\mathrm{YES}}



=



\frac{



150\cdot\frac{70}{150}



+



250\cdot\frac{75}{250}



+



100\cdot\frac{30}{100}



}{500}



}



$$



$$



=



\frac{70+75+30}{500}



=



\boxed{0.35}.



$$







\textbf{Step 2 --- CLT for the July proportion.}







Treating panellists as independent with estimated July YES probability $0.35$, for panel size $n=1000$,



$$



\boxed{



\bar Y_{\mathrm{July}}



\approx



\mathcal N



\left(



0.35,\,



\frac{0.35(0.65)}{1000}



\right).



}



$$







Thus



$$



\sigma



=



\sqrt{



\frac{0.35(0.65)}{1000}



}



\approx



0.015.



$$







\textbf{Step 3 --- evaluate the tail probability.}







$$



\boxed{



\hat q



=



P(\bar Y_{\mathrm{July}}>0.5)



\approx



1-\Phi



\left(



\frac{0.5-0.35}{0.015}



\right)



}



$$



$$



=



1-\Phi(10)



\approx



\boxed{0}.



$$







The exam statement appears internally inconsistent about the panel size, but the substantive conclusion is robust: an estimated YES probability of $0.35$ is sufficiently far below $0.50$ that the estimated majority probability is essentially zero under the stated large-panel approximations.







\textit{Possible extensions of the Markov-chain model:}



higher-order dependence ($r>1$), non-homogeneous transition matrices $P_t$, or individual-specific transition matrices allowing heterogeneity.            agrehpihdispoaidgahdisgphdghpidgspisghdpisdg

trash.title: tuning alfa in SES
trash.content:
In SES: 
$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 1$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx y_t$ (follows the data)

$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 0$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx$ constant

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Choosing $\alpha$ — grid search.}} Try a grid $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.99\}$. For each $\alpha$, compute the one-step-ahead forecasts on held-out data and evaluate one of:

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{0.b} \textbf{MAD} (Mean Absolute Deviation) --- the book's name; ML literature calls this \emph{MAE}:$$ \mathrm{MAD} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| y_t - \hat{y}_t \right| $$

\textbf{MSE} (Mean Squared Error):$$ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left( y_t - \hat{y}_t \right)^2 $$

\textbf{MAPE} (Mean Absolute Percentage Error):$$ \mathrm{MAPE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_t - \hat{y}_t}{y_t} \right| $$
\end{keydef}

Pick $\hat\alpha = \arg\min_\alpha \mathrm{(MAD\, /\, MSE\, /\, MAPE)}$. MAD is robust to outliers, MSE penalises large errors more heavily, MAPE is scale-free but blows up when $y_t \approx 0$.

trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.2 Asymptotic distributions.}}

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{19} Aim: asympthotic distribution of  $p_{i,j}$ and $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$


1) $(n_{i,1}, \dots, n_{i,M}) \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_{i,+};\, p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M})$. Notice that $n_{i,+}$ is random, as it depends on the sample. If we knew $n_{i,+}$, by the properties of the MLE of multinomial probabilities, we would have
\[
\mathbb{E}(\hat p_{i,j}) = p_{i,j}; \qquad V(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}; \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\, \hat p_{i,h}) = -\,\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}},
\]
and, the multinomial porporiton, conditional on ni+, by CLT would be distirbuted as multivariate gaussians

\textbf{Why?*}
2) \emph{Prerequisite --- pin down the initial mix.} Assume the empirical initial distribution converges to a fixed $\eta$:
\[ \frac{ \overbrace{n_h(0)}^{\text{n of indiv in state h at 0}} }{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{\eta_h}_{\text{initial probability of state $h$}}, \qquad h = 1, \dots, M. \]
(in a finite sample may differ.) Then let
\[
\underbrace{\varphi_i}_{\text{expected \# of visits to state $i$ of individual $k$ over full $T$}} \;=\; \sum_{h=1}^{M} \eta_h \sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{h,i}^{(t-1)}
\]
One can show that $n\varphi_i$ is the expected total number of observations in state $i$ for $t = 0, \dots, T-1$, and that
\[
\frac{n_{i,+}}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \varphi_i,
\]
so that, for large $n$, we have $n_{i,+} \approx n\varphi_i$. 
3) It can be proved that the rows of the estimated transition matrix $\widehat{\mathbf P}$ are asymptotically independent.

**HENCE, overall:**

\emph{Full row (joint).}
\[
(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})' \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}_M(\mathbf{p}_i,\, \Sigma),
\]
with mean vector $\mathbf{p}_i = (p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M})'$ and covariance matrix with elements
\[
V(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n\varphi_i}; \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\, \hat p_{i,h}) = -\,\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n\varphi_i}. \tag{5}
\]


\textbf{Asymptotic confidence interval (Wald).}
The marginal distribution of any one component is just the marginal of a multivariate Gaussian — and the marginal of a Gaussian is Gaussian, with mean and variance equal to the corresponding entry of the joint.
\[
\boxed{\;\hat p_{i,j} \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}}\;}
\]

\textbf{Tail probability (for forecasting questions).} For any $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, standardise to $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$:
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{P}(X > c) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\!\Bigl(Z > \frac{c - \mu}{\sigma}\Bigr) \;=\; 1 - \Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{c - \mu}{\sigma}\Bigr).\;}
\]
\emph{Used directly to estimate things like $\mathbb{P}(\text{July YES share} > 50\%)$: plug $\mu = \hat p_{\text{YES}}$, $\sigma = \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$, $c = 0.5$.}
\end{keydef}


*Why ?
\[ \hat p_{i,j} \;=\; \frac{n_{i,j}}{n_{i,+}} \;=\; \frac{1}{n_{i,+}} \sum_{m=1}^{n_{i,+}} X_m \;=\; \overline X, \]
which is exactly the sample mean of the Bernoulli atoms: $ X_m=\mathbf{1}\{\text{the }m\text{-th departure from }i\text{to }j\}$. RECALLING THAT: \emph{Mean and variance of a Bernoulli.} For $X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:
\[ \mathbb{E}[X] = p_{i,j}, \qquad V(X) = p_{i,j} - p_{i,j}^2 = p_{i,j}(1-p_{i,j}). \]
\emph{Distribution of the sample-mean estimator.} i.i.d.\ CLT then gives
\[ \sqrt{n_{i,+}}\,(\hat p_{i,j} - p_{i,j}) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\; p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})\bigr) \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \hat p_{i,j} \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(p_{i,j},\; \frac{p_{i,j}(1-p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}\right). \]
2) The full row is just a multinomial, where the expected value and vdariance of each entry is as in the bernoulli mean estimator, but additionally here we haev the covariance term.

\[ \sqrt{n_{i,+}}\,(\hat p_{i,j} - p_{i,j}) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\; p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})\bigr) \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \hat p_{i,j} \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(p_{i,j},\; \frac{p_{i,j}(1-p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}\right). \]
2) The full row is just a multinomial, where the expected value and vdariance of each entry is as in the bernoulli mean estimator, but additionally here we haev the covariance term.

trash.title: Asymptotics
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.2 Asymptotic distributions.}}

\begin{keydef}
\fcnum{19} Aim: asympthotic distribution of  $p_{i,j}$ and $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$


1) $(n_{i,1}, \dots, n_{i,M}) \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_{i,+};\, p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M})$. Notice that $n_{i,+}$ is random, as it depends on the sample. If we knew $n_{i,+}$, by the properties of the MLE of multinomial probabilities, we would have
\[
\mathbb{E}(\hat p_{i,j}) = p_{i,j}; \qquad V(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}; \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\, \hat p_{i,h}) = -\,\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}},
\]
and, the multinomial porporiton, conditional on ni+, by CLT would be distirbuted as multivariate gaussians

\textbf{Why?*}
2) \emph{Prerequisite --- pin down the initial mix.} Assume the empirical initial distribution converges to a fixed $\eta$:
\[ \frac{ \overbrace{n_h(0)}^{\text{n of indiv in state h at 0}} }{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{\eta_h}_{\text{initial probability of state $h$}}, \qquad h = 1, \dots, M. \]
(in a finite sample may differ.) Then let
\[
\underbrace{\varphi_i}_{\text{expected \# of visits to state $i$ of individual $k$ over full $T$}} \;=\; \sum_{h=1}^{M} \eta_h \sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{h,i}^{(t-1)}
\]
One can show that $n\varphi_i$ is the expected total number of observations in state $i$ for $t = 0, \dots, T-1$, and that
\[
\frac{n_{i,+}}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \varphi_i,
\]
so that, for large $n$, we have $n_{i,+} \approx n\varphi_i$. 
3) It can be proved that the rows of the estimated transition matrix $\widehat{\mathbf P}$ are asymptotically independent.

**HENCE, overall:**

\emph{Full row (joint).}
\[
(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})' \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}_M(\mathbf{p}_i,\, \Sigma),
\]
with mean vector $\mathbf{p}_i = (p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M})'$ and covariance matrix with elements
\[
V(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n\varphi_i}; \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\, \hat p_{i,h}) = -\,\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n\varphi_i}. \tag{5}
\]


\textbf{Asymptotic confidence interval (Wald).}
The marginal distribution of any one component is just the marginal of a multivariate Gaussian — and the marginal of a Gaussian is Gaussian, with mean and variance equal to the corresponding entry of the joint.
\[
\boxed{\;\hat p_{i,j} \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}}\;}
\]

\textbf{Tail probability (for forecasting questions).} For any $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, standardise to $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$:
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{P}(X > c) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\!\Bigl(Z > \frac{c - \mu}{\sigma}\Bigr) \;=\; 1 - \Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{c - \mu}{\sigma}\Bigr).\;}
\]
\emph{Used directly to estimate things like $\mathbb{P}(\text{July YES share} > 50\%)$: plug $\mu = \hat p_{\text{YES}}$, $\sigma = \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$, $c = 0.5$.}
\end{keydef}


*Why ?
\[ \hat p_{i,j} \;=\; \frac{n_{i,j}}{n_{i,+}} \;=\; \frac{1}{n_{i,+}} \sum_{m=1}^{n_{i,+}} X_m \;=\; \overline X, \]
which is exactly the sample mean of the Bernoulli atoms: $ X_m=\mathbf{1}\{\text{the }m\text{-th departure from }i\text{to }j\}$. RECALLING THAT: \emph{Mean and variance of a Bernoulli.} For $X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:
\[ \mathbb{E}[X] = p_{i,j}, \qquad V(X) = p_{i,j} - p_{i,j}^2 = p_{i,j}(1-p_{i,j}). \]
\emph{Distribution of the sample-mean estimator.} i.i.d.\ CLT then gives
\[ \sqrt{n_{i,+}}\,(\hat p_{i,j} - p_{i,j}) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\; p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})\bigr) \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \hat p_{i,j} \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(p_{i,j},\; \frac{p_{i,j}(1-p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}\right). \]
2) The full row is just a multinomial, where the expected value and vdariance of each entry is as in the bernoulli mean estimator, but additionally here we haev the covariance term.

nodes.title: Sep 2025 — Q1
nodes.content: In classic Statistics, a time series is regarded as a stochastic process. Explain: **(a)** What is a stochastic process? **(b)** Define a time series as a stochastic process. --- **Solution.** \textbf{(a)} A stochastic process is a sequence of random vectors $(Y_t)_{t\in T}$ indexed by time $t\in T$ (e.g.\ $T=\mathbb{N}$). It is fully specified by its finite-dimensional distributions $\{f_{Y_{t_1},\dots,Y_{t_k}}(y_1,\dots,y_k):k\ge 1,(t_1,\dots,t_k)\in T^k\}$ (Kolmogorov's extension theorem, given consistency). \textbf{(b)} A time series is a stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t\in T}$ with $Y_t\in\mathcal Y$; the data $(y_1,\dots,y_T)$ are a single \emph{finite realization} of one path. Inference from a single path is possible only under structural assumptions (stationarity, parametric dynamics).

nodes.title: May 2023 — Q1
nodes.content: What is a time series? An answer could be: "A time series is a sequence of observations taken over time." Are you happy with this definition? \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.6em] \item[A.] \textbf{Yes}, because: \item[B.] \textbf{No}, because: \item[C.] \textbf{Yes}, under the conditions: \end{itemize} --- **Solution.** \textbf{NO} (incomplete). A time series is the \emph{realization} of a stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t\in T}$ (keydef \textbf{1}--\textbf{2}). The bare "sequence of observations" misses the probabilistic model that gives meaning to mean, variance, ACVF, stationarity, inference.

nodes.title: Sep 2025 — Q2
nodes.content: Consider a univariate time series $(Y_t)_{t\ge 1}$. **(a)** Define its mean function and autocovariance function. **(b)** When is the time series (weakly) stationary? **(c)** Suppose that the time series is \textbf{not} stationary. Can you use an ARMA model for it? \emph{Start your reply with:} \textbf{YES, because\ldots, NO because\ldots, or YES but only if\ldots} --- **Solution.** \textbf{(a)} $\mu(t)=\mathbb{E}[Y_t]$; $\gamma(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_s,Y_t)$, a function of \emph{two} arguments. \textbf{(b)} Weakly stationary iff $\mathbb{E}[Y_t]$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y_tY_{t+h}]$ are finite and do not depend on $t$, for every $h$: $\mu(t)=\mu$, $\sigma^2(t)=\sigma^2$, $\gamma(t,t+h)=\tilde\gamma(h)$. \textbf{(c) NO}, because ARMA has \emph{constant} coefficients $(\phi_i,\theta_j,\sigma^2)$, hence constant mean/variance and lag-only ACVF; it cannot describe a non-stationary mean/variance. \textbf{YES, but only if} the non-stationarity is first removed: differencing $(1-B)^d$ for unit roots (ARIMA), $(1-B^s)$ for seasonality (SARIMA), or remove trend/seasonality and fit ARMA to the stationary residual.

nodes.title: Jun 2024 — Q1
nodes.content: Let $(Y_t)_{t\ge 1}$ be a univariate time series. **(a)** When is it \emph{(weakly) stationary}? **(b)** Provide an example of a stationary time series. --- **Solution.** \textbf{(a) Weak stationarity.} The series $(Y_t)$ is weakly (covariance-)stationary iff $\mathbb{E}[Y_t]$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y_tY_{t+h}]$ are finite and \emph{do not depend on $t$}, for every $h$: $$\mu(t)=\mu,\qquad \sigma^2(t)=\sigma^2,\qquad \gamma(t,t+h)=\tilde\gamma(h).$$ Equivalently, mean is constant and the autocovariance depends on the lag only. \textbf{(b) Two canonical examples.} (i) \emph{White noise.} $Y_t\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$: $\mu=0$, $\gamma(h)=\sigma^2\,\mathbf{1}\{h=0\}$ — manifestly $t$-free. (ii) \emph{Causal AR(1).} $Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, with $|\phi|<1$ and started in the stationary distribution (i.e.\ $Y_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2/(1-\phi^2))$). \emph{Why stationary:} by causal MA expansion $Y_t=\sum_{j\ge 0}\phi^j\varepsilon_{t-j}$ (geometric series converges since $|\phi|<1$), so $\mathbb{E}[Y_t]=0$ and $\gamma(h)=\sigma^2\phi^{|h|}/(1-\phi^2)$ — both $t$-free. \emph{R simulation:} `acf(y, lag.max=20) ## sample ACF should match phi^h / (1-phi^2)`

nodes.title: Theory — ACVF / correlogram — when defined?
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{THEORY --- ACVF / correlogram — when defined? [Topic: T2 — Stationarity, ACVF \& sample mean]}}

\textbf{1. Autocovariance function (ACVF) — population definition.}

For a univariate time series $(Y_t)_{t\in T}$ with $\mathbb{E}[Y_t^2]<\infty$ for all $t$, the \emph{autocovariance function} is
\[
\gamma(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_s,Y_t)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Y_s-\mu(s))(Y_t-\mu(t))\bigr],\qquad s,t\in T.
\]

\boxed{\;\gamma(s,t)\text{ is defined whenever the second moments are finite — \textbf{no} stationarity required.}\;}

It is a function of \emph{two} arguments. The autocorrelation function (ACF) is the normalised version
$\rho(s,t)=\gamma(s,t)/\sqrt{\gamma(s,s)\gamma(t,t)}$.

\textbf{2. What stationarity changes (\emph{not} whether $\gamma$ exists, but how it depends on $(s,t)$).}

Under weak stationarity (see t2a), the ACVF reduces to a function of the lag only:
\[
\gamma(s,t)=\tilde\gamma(t-s)=\tilde\gamma(h),\qquad h=t-s.
\]
i.e.\ a 1-argument function. Stationarity is therefore the assumption that makes "the autocovariance at lag $h$" — a single number — well-posed.

\emph{Properties of $\tilde\gamma$ under weak stationarity}: $\tilde\gamma(0)=\sigma^2\ge 0$; $\tilde\gamma(-h)=\tilde\gamma(h)$; $|\tilde\gamma(h)|\le\tilde\gamma(0)$ (Cauchy–Schwarz); positive semi-definite ($\sum_{i,j}c_ic_j\tilde\gamma(t_i-t_j)\ge 0$).

\textbf{3. So: "the ACVF can be defined only if the series is stationary" — TRUE or FALSE?}

\boxed{\;\textbf{FALSE / NO.}\;}\quad The two-argument $\gamma(s,t)$ exists for any second-order process. Stationarity is needed only to \emph{reduce} the ACVF to a single-argument lag function $\tilde\gamma(h)$ — \emph{not} to define it.

\textbf{4. Sample ACVF (correlogram) — estimator.}

Given data $y_1,\dots,y_T$ from a univariate series with sample mean $\bar Y_T=T^{-1}\sum_t Y_t$, the standard \emph{sample autocovariance} at lag $h\ge 0$ is
\[
\widehat\gamma(h)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T-|h|}(Y_t-\bar Y_T)(Y_{t+|h|}-\bar Y_T),\qquad |h|<T,
\]
and the sample autocorrelation is $\widehat\rho(h)=\widehat\gamma(h)/\widehat\gamma(0)$. The \emph{correlogram} is the plot $h\mapsto\widehat\rho(h)$ (with 95\% confidence bands $\pm 1.96/\sqrt T$ under the white-noise null).

\textbf{5. When does the correlogram make sense as an estimator?}

The sample ACVF \emph{pools across $t$}: it averages many products $(Y_t-\bar Y)(Y_{t+h}-\bar Y)$ to estimate a \emph{single} quantity. This pooling is meaningful only if there is a single quantity to estimate — i.e.\ only if $\gamma(t,t+h)$ does \emph{not} depend on $t$. That is exactly weak stationarity.

Furthermore, for $\widehat\gamma(h)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\tilde\gamma(h)$ (consistency), we also need \emph{ergodicity}: time-averages converge to ensemble-averages,
\[
\frac{1}{T-|h|}\sum_{t=1}^{T-|h|}(Y_t-\mu)(Y_{t+|h|}-\mu)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\tilde\gamma(h).
\]
For stationary Gaussian processes, ergodicity follows from $\tilde\gamma(h)\to 0$ as $h\to\infty$ — a mild mixing condition.

\boxed{\;\text{Correlogram interpretable as an estimate of "the ACVF" }\Longleftrightarrow\;\text{weak stationarity + ergodicity.}\;}

If $(Y_t)$ is \emph{not} stationary (trend, seasonality, drift), then $\gamma(t,t+h)$ depends on $t$. The sample ACVF averages over inhomogeneous quantities and has no clean population target — the correlogram becomes a misleading diagnostic ("spurious autocorrelation"). Classic symptom: correlogram of an integrated series decays linearly to zero rather than geometrically, reflecting the unit root rather than any meaningful $\tilde\gamma(h)$.

\textbf{6. Worked micro-example.}

For a causal AR(1) $Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ with $|\phi|=0.7$, $\sigma^2=1$, the population ACVF is $\tilde\gamma(h)=0.7^{|h|}/(1-0.49)\approx 1.96\cdot 0.7^{|h|}$. The correlogram from $T=500$ should overlay these values within $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{500}\approx 0.088$ bands at long lags. For a random walk $Y_t=\sum_{s\le t}\varepsilon_s$, the sample ACF stays close to 1 for many lags before slowly tailing off — diagnostic of non-stationarity, not of "the ACVF" of the series.

\textbf{7. R — computing and plotting the correlogram.}

\textbf{8. Summary — answers to the two recurring exam questions.}

\emph{(a) "The ACVF can be defined only if the series is stationary." Correct?}\quad
\boxed{\;\textbf{NO.}\;}\;\;The ACVF $\gamma(s,t)$ is defined for any second-order process. Stationarity merely reduces it from a 2-argument function to a 1-argument lag function $\tilde\gamma(h)$.

\emph{(b) "The correlogram can be used to estimate the ACVF only if the series is stationary." Correct?}\quad
\boxed{\;\textbf{YES (essentially).}\;}\;\;The correlogram pools across $t$ to estimate one number per lag; this targets a well-defined quantity only when $\gamma(t,t+h)$ depends on the lag alone, i.e.\ under weak stationarity. Add ergodicity for consistency.

\textbf{Exam pointers.}
\begin{itemize}
\item[$\triangleright$] Used in \texttt{exam\_may\_2025\_q1}: (a) "ACVF defined only if stationary?" — NO, defined whenever $\mathbb{E}[Y_t^2]<\infty$. (b) "Correlogram can estimate ACVF only if stationary?" — YES, because pooling across $t$ is meaningful only when $\gamma$ depends on the lag alone; plus ergodicity for consistency.
\item[$\triangleright$] Used in \texttt{exam\_may\_2022\_q2}: same as (a) — NO, the ACVF $\gamma(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_s,Y_t)$ is defined whenever second moments are finite.
\item[$\triangleright$] Used in \texttt{exam\_may\_2021\_q2}: same as (a) — NO.
\end{itemize}

nodes.title: Master — ACVF / correlogram — when defined?
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MASTER --- ACVF / correlogram — when defined?}} ---
≥3 ex (Q1) The autocovariance function (acf) can be defined only if the time series is stationary. Answer as either: A. Yes, because: ... or B. No, because: ... [May 2025 Q1a, May 2022 Q2, May 2021 Q2] \textbf{B. NO.} The autocovariance function \[ \gamma(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_s,Y_t)=\mathbb{E}\big[(Y_s-\mu(s))(Y_t-\mu(t))\big] \] is well-defined for \emph{any} stochastic process satisfying $\mathbb{E}[Y_t^2]<\infty$ for all $t$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y_s),\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)<\infty$ and Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\gamma(s,t)|\le\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y_s)\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)}<\infty$. Stationarity is \emph{not} required for the ACVF to \textbf{exist}. \emph{What stationarity actually buys you} is a \textbf{simplification}, not the existence: - Without stationarity, $\gamma(s,t)$ is a function of \emph{two} arguments. - Under weak stationarity, $\gamma(s,t)=\gamma(s+k,t+k)$ for any shift $k$, hence depends only on the lag $h=t-s$: write $\tilde\gamma(h)=\gamma(t,t+h)$ — a function of \emph{one} argument. \emph{Counterexample for the "Yes" camp.} The random walk $Y_t=\sum_{i\le t}\varepsilon_i$ with $\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ is \emph{not} stationary, yet \[ \gamma(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}\Big(\sum_{i\le s}\varepsilon_i,\sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j\Big)=\sigma^2\min(s,t) \] is perfectly well-defined — it just depends on both $s$ and $t$. \emph{R analogue:} `cov(y[1:499], y[2:500]) ## sample lag-1 covariance — finite, defined`
≥1 ex (Q2) The correlogram can be used to estimate the acf only if the time series is stationary. Answer as either: A. Yes, because: ... or B. No, because: ... [May 2025 Q1b] \textbf{A. YES} — essentially. The correlogram is the sample ACVF \[ \hat\gamma(h)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T-|h|}(Y_t-\bar Y)(Y_{t+|h|}-\bar Y), \] (and the sample ACF $\hat\rho(h)=\hat\gamma(h)/\hat\gamma(0)$). It \emph{pools across $t$} to produce a single estimate of "the lag-$h$ autocovariance". That pooling is meaningful only if the underlying ACVF actually depends on the lag alone — i.e.\ under \textbf{weak stationarity}. Otherwise different summands $(Y_t-\bar Y)(Y_{t+|h|}-\bar Y)$ are estimating \emph{different} population quantities $\gamma(t,t+h)$, and their average has no clean interpretation as "$\hat\gamma(h)$". A second condition is needed for \textbf{consistency}: \textbf{ergodicity}, so that the time-average $T^{-1}\sum_t\to\mathbb{E}$ as $T\to\infty$. (Stationarity alone implies unbiasedness — apart from the small-sample bias from dividing by $T$ rather than $T-|h|$ — but not consistency.) \emph{Summary.} - \emph{Definition of ACVF:} needs $\mathbb{E}[Y_t^2]<\infty$ only. - \emph{Existence of a single lag-only function:} needs weak stationarity. - \emph{Consistency of the correlogram:} needs weak stationarity + ergodicity. \emph{Practical implication.} If you plot \texttt{acf(y)} on a non-stationary series (trended Nile, random walk), you'll see an artificially slow decay — that's the diagnostic. Difference / detrend first. %%RBLOCK%% `acf(Nile) ## slow decay — flags non-stationarity` `acf(diff(Nile)) ## post-differencing, behaves like stationary` %%/RBLOCK%%
\textbf{Linked exams:} \texttt{exam_may_2025_q1}, \texttt{exam_may_2022_q2}, \texttt{exam_may_2021_q2}.

nodes.title: May 2025 — Q1
nodes.content: Consider a univariate time series $(Y_t)_{t\ge 1}$. **(a)** The \emph{autocovariance function} (acf) can be defined only if the time series is stationary. Answer as either: **A. Yes, because:** ... or **B. No, because:** ... **(b)** The correlogram can be used to estimate the acf only if the time series is stationary. Answer as either: **A. Yes, because:** ... or **B. No, because:** ... --- **Solution.** \textbf{(a) NO.} The autocovariance function is defined as $\gamma(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_s,Y_t)$ for \emph{any} time series with $\mathbb{E}[Y_t^2]<\infty$ — it is a function of two arguments $(s,t)$. Stationarity is \emph{not} required to define it; it merely allows the reduction to a 1-argument function $\gamma(h)=\gamma(t,t+h)$ of the lag $h$ only (since under weak stationarity $\gamma(s,t)$ depends only on $|s-t|$). \textbf{(b) YES} (essentially). The correlogram estimator $$\hat\gamma(h)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T-|h|}(Y_t-\bar Y)(Y_{t+|h|}-\bar Y)$$ \emph{pools} across $t$ to estimate one function of the lag. This is meaningful only if the true ACVF depends solely on the lag — i.e.\ under (weak) stationarity. Plus ergodicity is needed for consistency (the time-average $T^{-1}\sum_t\to\mathbb{E}$). Without these, $\hat\gamma(h)$ has no clean interpretation as an estimate of "the" autocovariance. \emph{R:}

Is that correct? \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.6em] \item[A.] \textbf{Yes}, because: \item[B.] \textbf{No}, because: \end{itemize} --- **Solution.** \textbf{NO}, same as Exam 3 Q1a.
